title: The Seventh Month: Trumpets, Atonement, and Booths
summary: The calendar of public offerings continues into the seventh month, the most festival-filled of Israel's year. The first day is a day of trumpet blasts, the tenth is the day when the people humble themselves (the Day of Atonement), and from the fifteenth comes a seven-day feast, the Feast of Tabernacles, with a descending number of bulls each day and a closing assembly on the eighth day.
story: Chapter 28 laid out the daily, weekly, and monthly offerings and the feasts of the spring. This chapter completes the calendar with the autumn feasts of the seventh month, and verses 39-40 close the whole two-chapter unit. For the new generation camped on the plains of Moab, the calendar describes a future life in the land, marked by harvests they have not yet gathered. The seventh month, in particular, gathers up the themes of Israel's story: a summons (trumpets), cleansing from sin (atonement), and joyful remembrance of God's care in the wilderness (booths). The next chapter turns from public offerings to the private vows individuals make, which verse 39 has just mentioned.
historical:
The seventh month (later called Tishri) falls in September or October, at the end of the agricultural year, when the grapes and olives were gathered. The feasts of this month were among the great public occasions of Israel's worship. Solomon dedicated the temple at the feast of the seventh month (1 Kings 8:2), and after the exile Ezra read the law to the people on the first day of the seventh month and led them to rediscover the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8). The first day of the seventh month later became Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, though in the Torah it is simply a day of trumpet blasts. The tenth day became Yom Kippur, still the most solemn day of the Jewish year.

The calendar describes the offerings of a settled people, with herds large enough to supply seventy-one bulls over eight days in the Feast of Tabernacles alone, plus rams, lambs, and goats. It looks forward to the prosperity of the land, not the scarcity of the desert.
cultural:
Three different feasts crowd this month, and each had its own character. The text of the day of trumpet blasts (verse 1) does not name the instrument, but Jewish practice has long used the ram's horn, the shofar, whose sound called assemblies, announced kings, and signaled war. Here it summons Israel before God. The tenth day required the people to humble themselves (verse 7), which Jewish tradition has understood as fasting and self-denial; its full ritual, with the high priest entering the Most Holy Place and the scapegoat sent into the wilderness, is described in Leviticus 16. The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths, was a harvest festival at which Israel lived for a week in temporary shelters to remember the wilderness years (Leviticus 23:42-43). It was the most joyful feast of the year.

The sacrifices at Tabernacles are strikingly large: thirteen bulls on the first day, then one fewer each day until seven on the seventh, a total of seventy. Later rabbinic tradition, recorded in the Talmud, connected the seventy bulls with the seventy nations listed in Genesis 10 and understood them as offered on behalf of all the peoples of the world. That reading is not stated in Numbers, but it shows how Jewish readers pondered the number.
literary: The chapter follows the same formula as chapter 28: date, holy assembly, rest from work, a list of animals, their grain and drink offerings, a goat for a sin offering, and the reminder that all this is “in addition to the regular burnt offering.” The Tabernacles section (verses 12-38) is the longest and most patterned stretch of the calendar. Day by day the number of bulls drops by one (thirteen, twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven), while the rams stay at two and the lambs at fourteen. The count of bulls ends at seven on the seventh day, and the whole festival totals seventy bulls, fourteen rams, and ninety-eight lambs, all multiples of seven. The eighth day stands apart, returning to the modest pattern of one bull, one ram, and seven lambs. The closing verses (39-40) summarize both chapters and remind the reader that these public offerings do not replace the vows and freewill offerings of individuals.

outline.t: The first day of the seventh month: a day of trumpet blasts
The tenth day: the people humble themselves
The Feast of Tabernacles, first day
The second through seventh days, with one fewer bull each day
The eighth day: a solemn assembly

doctrines.note: The tenth day of the seventh month, set out fully in Leviticus 16, was the day of atonement for the whole nation. Here it appears within the calendar, with its own burnt offerings and sin offerings, a reminder that the year of worship was built around God's provision for sin.
On the tenth day Israel must humble itself and do no work. Repentance is not left to private feeling alone; it is given a day, shared by the whole people.
The Feast of Tabernacles combined harvest joy with the memory of living in shelters in the wilderness. Israel was taught to see its abundance and its years of dependence as the work of the same God.

words.note: Teruah, a shout or blast. The word is used for a battle cry, a shout of joy, and the sounding of horns or trumpets. The first day of the seventh month is literally a day of blasting. It is a summons, calling the people to attention before the LORD.

Anah, to humble or afflict. On the tenth day Israel must humble itself (literally afflict their souls). The word describes bringing low, and in this setting it was understood as fasting and self-denial. It is a bodily act of repentance, done by the whole community together.

Atsarah, a solemn or closing assembly. It names the eighth day that ends the Feast of Tabernacles, a day of rest and gathering after the week of celebration. In Jewish practice it became Shemini Atzeret, the Eighth Day of Assembly.

christ: The feasts of this chapter are woven into the New Testament's picture of Jesus. Hebrews reads the Day of Atonement as a shadow of Christ's work, describing him as a high priest who entered not an earthly sanctuary but heaven itself, once for all, by his own blood (Hebrews 9:11-12, 24-26). John sets one of Jesus' great public declarations at the Feast of Tabernacles: on its last and greatest day Jesus stood up and called out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37). John also says that the Word “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), using a Greek verb related to the word for tent, which many interpreters connect with the tabernacle and the booths. The prophets expected the Feast of Tabernacles to be kept by the nations in the age to come (Zechariah 14:16), and the New Testament sees the gathering of the nations beginning in Christ. These are connections the later writers draw, not predictions made in the text of Numbers.
questions: The seventh month moves from a summons, to repentance, to a week of joy. What does that order suggest about the relationship between repentance and celebration?
At the Feast of Tabernacles Israel lived in temporary shelters to remember their dependence on God in the wilderness. What practices help you remember times when you had to depend on him?
Why do you think the Day of Atonement was set in the middle of a month of festivals rather than kept separate from them?
